standard.title: Develop and modify civic questions
standard.description: develop and modify questions to investigate Australia's political and legal systems, and contemporary civic issues
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have developed and modified questions to investigate Australia's political and legal systems and contemporary civic issues at Year 9 (AC9HC9S01). They can formulate sub-questions and revisit questions based on new information.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students develop and modify questions that guide sustained civic inquiry, generating productive sub-questions and revising the inquiry based on evidence gathered.

nodes.label: Framing an investigable civic question
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop an overarching inquiry question about Australia's political or legal system or a contemporary civic issue that is specific, investigable, and productively open.
nodes.minimum_width: Develop one overarching inquiry question about a political, legal or civic issue that is investigable — not too broad, not yes/no.
nodes.typical_width: Develop an overarching inquiry question about Australia's political or legal system or a contemporary civic issue that is specific, investigable, and productively open — able to sustain sub-questions and structured inquiry.
wider: Practise framing questions across multiple civic domains (political systems, legal rights, civic participation) and evaluate which framing opens the richest inquiry
Examine examples of civic inquiry questions that led to significant public policy change and analyse what made them productive
Develop and compare overarching questions from the perspectives of different civic actors (e.g. a citizen, an NGO, the government) on the same issue
nodes.hinge_reason: A poorly framed overarching question makes the entire inquiry phase structurally unsound — sub-questions cannot compensate for a question that is too broad, too narrow, or not genuinely investigable. Phase collapse begins here.

response_modes.reason: Teach the criteria for a productive inquiry question explicitly — scope, investigability, openness — before students attempt to frame one. Model the difference between strong and weak framing.

success_criteria: Develops an overarching inquiry question about a political, legal or civic issue
The question is neither too broad nor a yes/no question — it is genuinely investigable
Can explain what the question is asking and why it matters civically

nodes.label: Generating connected sub-questions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop a range of sub-questions connected to the overarching question that collectively structure a productive investigation.
nodes.minimum_width: Develop at least three sub-questions connected to the overarching question that together cover different aspects of the investigation.
nodes.typical_width: Develop a range of sub-questions connected to the overarching question — for example, addressing representation, equality, accountability, and accessibility — and explain how the sub-questions collectively structure the inquiry.
wider: Develop sub-questions that deliberately seek out different perspectives — including those of groups whose voices are less commonly represented in civic debate
Practise generating sub-questions across multiple overarching questions and evaluate which sets of sub-questions best support a structured investigation
Design a full inquiry framework showing how sub-questions connect to different evidence sources

response_modes.reason: Students often generate sub-questions that are essentially restatements of the main question or that only address one dimension. Scaffold the process of mapping different dimensions of an inquiry (e.g. structural, representational, evaluative) before students generate sub-questions independently.

success_criteria: Develops at least three sub-questions connected to the overarching question
Sub-questions address different aspects of the investigation (not all asking the same thing)
Can explain how each sub-question contributes to answering the overarching question

nodes.label: Revising questions based on evidence
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can revisit and modify their inquiry questions based on further information collected, including identifying whether different groups hold particular views that require the question to be refined.
nodes.minimum_width: Modify at least one inquiry question (overarching or sub-question) in response to evidence collected, with an explanation of why the modification improves the inquiry.
nodes.typical_width: Revisit the inquiry questions based on further collection of information and modify them to reflect emerging insights — including consideration of whether different groups in society hold particular views on the issue being investigated that require the question framing to be refined.
wider: Trace the evolution of inquiry questions across a complete investigation and reflect on how evidence-driven revision improved the quality of the final inquiry
Practise modifying questions when evidence reveals that the original framing contained an unexamined assumption
Investigate how questions in a real civic inquiry (e.g. a parliamentary inquiry) are modified as submissions and evidence come in

response_modes.reason: This node integrates questioning skill with the evidence-gathering process — students must hold both the inquiry framework and the emerging evidence in mind simultaneously. Teaching investment is in helping students see modification as a sign of productive inquiry, not failure.

success_criteria: Modifies at least one inquiry question in response to evidence collected
Provides a clear explanation of why the modification improves the inquiry
Shows awareness that different groups may hold different views that affect how the question is framed
